# AI Memory Games for Dementia Care: What Families Should Know

> **In short:** SAP, EY, and the app Memory Lane Games have built an AI prototype that turns a person's own life stories into personalized memory games for dementia care. It's still a prototype, not something you can download today, but it points to where caregiving tools are heading.

If you've ever sat next to a parent or grandparent who doesn't quite remember your name anymore, you know how painful those moments feel. A new project is trying to ease that — by using AI to build memory games out of the actual life of the person playing them.

## What the project is

Memory Lane Games is a small company that already makes simple memory games for people living with dementia. Their existing app uses gentle questions like "What street did you grow up on?" or "What was your first job?" — prompts a caregiver can use during a visit.

The new piece is a collaboration with SAP (the big enterprise software company) and EY (the consulting firm). Together they've built an **AI prototype** — a working-but-early version of a tool that can take stories about someone's life and turn them into new, personalized memory activities automatically.

In plain terms: instead of a caregiver sitting down to write out twenty questions about Mom's childhood, the AI would help generate them from the stories a family has already shared. A granddaughter could upload old letters, or a son could type in a few memories, and the system would build a custom set of questions around them.

## Why personalization matters

Dementia affects everyone differently. Some people lose short-term memory first but keep childhood memories sharp for years. Others struggle with language or get frustrated by anything that feels like a test. Generic trivia games often miss the mark — they're too random, too unfamiliar, too easy to dismiss as "not for me."

When the questions come from a person's own life — their wedding, their first car, the street they lived on at age eight — the brain has more hooks to grab onto. Caregivers and researchers have known this for decades. Old photos, familiar songs, and personal stories often spark moments of clarity that nothing else does.

What AI adds here is speed and scale. A family could feed in stories over time and the tool could keep building fresh activities from them, so the games don't go stale the way a printed quiz book does.

## What this means for you

- **If you're caring for a parent or grandparent:** You don't need to wait for this tool. The ideas behind it — using personal stories as memory prompts — work today, with a photo album, a favorite song, or a stack of old letters. Try starting with one specific memory and see what reaction you get.
- **If you work in caregiving or senior care:** Keep an eye on Memory Lane Games and similar tools. Personalized AI-generated activities could become part of standard care, especially in facilities where staff don't always know each resident's full history.
- **If you're just curious about where AI is heading:** This is a quieter, more human example of what AI can do. It's not about replacing human contact — it's about giving families and caregivers more raw material to work with.

A note worth repeating: none of this replaces medical advice. If someone you love is showing signs of memory loss, the right first step is a conversation with their doctor, not a new app.

## Wrap-up

Personalized memory games won't cure dementia — nothing does yet. But they can give families a way to stay connected during a stage of life when connection gets harder. The AI prototype from Memory Lane Games, SAP, and EY is one sign of where this is going. The bigger takeaway for any family is simple: the stories you already have may be the best tool you own.
